items.readable_text:
Content:
A common type of problem is to match a given rational function [MATH: f(x)] with its graph.

Content:
To solve these types of problems, we determine the properties of the given function and then eliminate any options that do not have the desired properties.

Content:
When referring to the properties of rational functions, we usually mean the following:

Content:
- [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-intercepts
- vertical and horizontal asymptotes
- holes of the function

Content:
Let's see some examples.

items.title: Identifying the Graph of a Rational Function That Does Not Contain Holes

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

[IMG: /graphics/36df7d3182a051e572810d237668a143]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we denote [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}.]

To determine the correct graph, we follow four steps:

  • Step 1: We find the [MATH: y]-intercept. To do this, we evaluate [MATH: f(0)\mathbin{:}] [MATH: f(x)|= (5)/(x^{2} + 4x − 5); f(0)|= (5)/((0)^{2} + 4(0) − 5); f(0)|= (5)/(− 5); f(0)|= − 1] So, the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: (0,-1).]

  • Step 2: We find the [MATH: x]-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x.]

    In this case, the numerator is a constant, and so there are no [MATH: x]-intercepts.

  • Step 3: We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we need to set the denominator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}] [MATH: x^{2} + 4x − 5|= 0; (x + 5)(x − 1)|= 0] Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are [MATH: x=-5] and [MATH: x=1.]

  • Step 4: We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is [MATH: x^2] in this case: [MATH: f(x)|= (5)/(x^{2} + 4x − 5); = (((5)/(x^{2})))/((1 + (4)/(x) − (5)/(x^{2})))] Now, as [MATH: |x|] gets very large, [MATH: \dfrac{5}{x^2}] and [MATH: \dfrac{4}{x}] become very small. Therefore, as [MATH: |x|\to\infty,] we have [MATH: f(x)|≈ (0)/(1 + 0 − 0) = 0.] So, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y = 0.]

Finally, among the options given, only graph I satisfies the above conditions:

items.title: Identifying the Graph of a Given Rational Function Containing One Hole

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^2 + 2x}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^2 + 2x}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

[IMG: /graphics/28fc40db21ca507afdb8e145d302c746]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we denote [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^2 + 2x} = \dfrac{x(x - 1)}{x(x+2)}.]

Notice that the numerator and denominator both have [MATH: x] as a common factor. Setting this common factor equal to zero and solving for [MATH: x] gives [MATH: %x - 2 = 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x= 2. x = 0.] Therefore, the function has a hole at [MATH: x=0.]

To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole, we find the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x)] and evaluate it at the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the hole.

Finding the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x),] we get [MATH: F(x)|= (x(x − 1))/(x(x + 2)); = (x(x − 1))/(x(x + 2)); = (x − 1)/(x + 2).]

The [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole is given by [MATH: F(0)|= (0 − 1)/(0 + 2); = − (1)/(2).]

So, the coordinates of the hole are [MATH: \left(0,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right).]

Now, to determine the correct graph, we follow four steps with the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x){:}]

  • Step 1: We find the [MATH: y]-intercept. However, since [MATH: x=0] is a hole, there is no [MATH: y]-intercept.

  • Step 2: We find the [MATH: x]-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: x − 1|= 0; x|= 1] So, the [MATH: x]-intercept is [MATH: (1,0).]

  • Step 3: We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we need to set the denominator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}] [MATH: x + 2|= 0; x|= − 2] Therefore, the vertical asymptote is [MATH: x=-2.]

  • Step 4: We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is [MATH: x] in this case: [MATH: F(x)|= (x − 1)/(x + 2); = ((1 − (1)/(x)))/((1 + (2)/(x)))] Now, as [MATH: |x|] gets very large, [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x}] and [MATH: \dfrac{2}{x}] becomes very small. Therefore, as [MATH: |x|\to\infty,] we have [MATH: F(x)|≈ (1 − 0)/(1 + 0) = 1.] So, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y = 1.]

Finally, among the options given, only graph III satisfies the above conditions:

items.title: Identifying a Rational Function Containing a Cubic Denominator

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y =\dfrac{4x^2-4}{x^3-x^2-9x+9} ?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y =\dfrac{4x^2-4}{x^3-x^2-9x+9} ?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

[IMG: /graphics/19c32f9d35fd39807e3c9b64c083896e]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we define the function [MATH: f(x)] and factor the numerator and denominator. [MATH: f(x)|= (4x^{2} − 4)/(x^{3} − x^{2} − 9x + 9); = (4(x^{2} − 1))/(x^{2}(x − 1) − 9(x − 1)); = (4(x − 1)(x + 1))/((x − 1)(x^{2} − 9)); = (4(x − 1)(x + 1))/((x − 1)(x + 3)(x − 3))]

Notice that the numerator and denominator both have [MATH: (x-1)] as a common factor. Setting this common factor equal to zero and solving for [MATH: x] gives [MATH: x - 1 = 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x= 1.] Therefore, the function has a hole at [MATH: x=1.]

To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole, we find the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x)] and evaluate it at the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the hole.

Finding the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x),] we get

[MATH: F(x)|= (4(x − 1)(x + 1))/((x − 1)(x + 3)(x − 3)); = (4(x − 1)(x + 1))/((x − 1)(x + 3)(x − 3)); = (4(x + 1))/((x + 3)(x − 3)).]

The [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole is given by [MATH: F(1)|= (4(1 + 1))/((1 + 3)(1 − 3)); = (8)/(− 8); = − 1.]

So, the coordinates of the hole are [MATH: (1,-1).]

Now, to determine the correct graph, we follow four steps with the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x){:}]

  • Step 1: We find the [MATH: y]-intercept. To do this, we evaluate [MATH: F(0){:}] [MATH: F(x)|= (4(x + 1))/((x + 3)(x − 3)); F(0)|= (4(0 + 1))/((0 + 3)(0 − 3)); = − (4)/(9)] So, the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: \left(0,-\dfrac{4}{9}\right).]

  • Step 2: We find the [MATH: x]-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: 4(x + 1)|= 0; x|= − 1] So, the [MATH: x]-intercept is [MATH: (-1,0).]

  • Step 3: We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}] [MATH: (x + 3)(x − 3)|= 0; x|= − 3, 3] Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are [MATH: x=-3] and [MATH: x=3.]

  • Step 4: We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is [MATH: x^2] in this case: [MATH: F(x)|= (4(x + 1))/((x + 3)(x − 3)); = (4x + 4)/(x^{2} − 9); = (((4)/(x) + (4)/(x^{2})))/((1 − (9)/(x^{2})))] Now, as [MATH: |x|] gets very large, [MATH: \dfrac{4}{x},] [MATH: \dfrac{4}{x^2},] and [MATH: \dfrac{9}{x^2}] becomes very small. Therefore, as [MATH: |x|\to\infty,] we have [MATH: F(x)|≈ (0 + 0)/(1 − 0) = 0.] So, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y = 0.]

Finally, among the options given, only graph III satisfies the above conditions:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A common type of problem is to match a given rational function [MATH: f(x)] with its graph.

Content:
To solve these types of problems, we determine the properties of the given function and then eliminate any options that do not have the desired properties.

Content:
When referring to the properties of rational functions, we usually mean the following:

Content:
- [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-intercepts
- vertical and horizontal asymptotes
- holes of the function

Content:
Let's see some examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Graph of a Rational Function That Does Not Contain Holes

Example Prompt:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

[IMG: /graphics/36df7d3182a051e572810d237668a143]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we denote [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}.]

To determine the correct graph, we follow four steps:

- Step 1: We find the [MATH: y]-intercept. To do this, we evaluate [MATH: f(0)\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f(x)|= (5)/(x^{2} + 4x − 5); f(0)|= (5)/((0)^{2} + 4(0) − 5); f(0)|= (5)/(− 5); f(0)|= − 1]
So, the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: (0,-1).]
- Step 2: We find the [MATH: x]-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x.]

In this case, the numerator is a constant, and so there are no [MATH: x]-intercepts.
- Step 3: We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we need to set the denominator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: x^{2} + 4x − 5|= 0; (x + 5)(x − 1)|= 0]
Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are [MATH: x=-5] and [MATH: x=1.]
- Step 4: We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is [MATH: x^2] in this case:
[MATH: f(x)|= (5)/(x^{2} + 4x − 5); = (((5)/(x^{2})))/((1 + (4)/(x) − (5)/(x^{2})))]
Now, as [MATH: |x|] gets very large, [MATH: \dfrac{5}{x^2}] and [MATH: \dfrac{4}{x}] become very small. Therefore, as [MATH: |x|\to\infty,] we have
[MATH: f(x)|≈ (0)/(1 + 0 − 0) = 0.]
So, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y = 0.]

Finally, among the options given, only graph I satisfies the above conditions:

[IMG: /graphics/c77dddbdff5993543004ff05dcea7ffb]

Item 5 — Example: Identifying the Graph of a Given Rational Function Containing One Hole

Example Prompt:
Which of the following is the graph of the function [MATH: y = \dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^2 + 2x}?]

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

[IMG: /graphics/28fc40db21ca507afdb8e145d302c746]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we denote
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^2 + 2x}
= \dfrac{x(x - 1)}{x(x+2)}.]

Notice that the numerator and denominator both have [MATH: x] as a common factor. Setting this common factor equal to zero and solving for [MATH: x] gives
[MATH: %x - 2 = 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x= 2.
x = 0.]
Therefore, the function has a hole at [MATH: x=0.]

To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole, we find the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x)] and evaluate it at the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the hole.

Finding the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x),] we get
[MATH: F(x)|= (x(x − 1))/(x(x + 2)); = (x(x − 1))/(x(x + 2)); = (x − 1)/(x + 2).]

The [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole is given by
[MATH: F(0)|= (0 − 1)/(0 + 2); = − (1)/(2).]

So, the coordinates of the hole are [MATH: \left(0,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right).]

Now, to determine the correct graph, we follow four steps with the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x){:}]

- Step 1: We find the [MATH: y]-intercept. However, since [MATH: x=0] is a hole, there is no [MATH: y]-intercept.
- Step 2: We find the [MATH: x]-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: x − 1|= 0; x|= 1]
So, the [MATH: x]-intercept is [MATH: (1,0).]
- Step 3: We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we need to set the denominator equal to zero and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: x + 2|= 0; x|= − 2]
Therefore, the vertical asymptote is [MATH: x=-2.]
- Step 4: We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is [MATH: x] in this case:
[MATH: F(x)|= (x − 1)/(x + 2); = ((1 − (1)/(x)))/((1 + (2)/(x)))]
Now, as [MATH: |x|] gets very large, [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x}] and [MATH: \dfrac{2}{x}] becomes very small. Therefore, as [MATH: |x|\to\infty,] we have
[MATH: F(x)|≈ (1 − 0)/(1 + 0) = 1.]
So, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y = 1.]

Finally, among the options given, only graph III satisfies the above conditions:

[IMG: /graphics/0e813f542ac7fe8957b7dbcfaf94caac]
